guideline_source: FAST Criteria + NIH Stroke Scale + AHA/ASA Guidelines
description: Rapid stroke recognition using FAST criteria and NIH Stroke Scale for assessment. Time-critical condition where 'Time is Brain' - every minute counts for treatment eligibility.

decision_rules.evidence_text: Unilateral facial weakness has LR+ of 5.7 for stroke. Ask patient to smile - look for asymmetry.
Unilateral arm weakness has LR+ of 3.2 for stroke. Ask patient to hold both arms up for 10 seconds - look for drift.

decision_rules.description: Slurred speech or inability to speak
decision_rules.evidence_text: Speech abnormality has LR+ of 3.4 for stroke. Ask patient to repeat a simple phrase - listen for slurring or wrong words.

decision_rules.description: Time of symptom onset and urgency of action

criteria.name: Symptom onset time
criteria.note: Determines eligibility for tPA (< 4.5 hours) and thrombectomy (< 24 hours)

decision_rules.evidence_text: IV tPA effective within 4.5 hours (NNT=10). Thrombectomy for LVO effective up to 24 hours in selected patients.

decision_rules.description: Sudden severe headache - worst of life
decision_rules.evidence_text: Thunderclap headache has 12-25% probability of SAH. Negative CT within 6 hours has >98% sensitivity; if later, LP required to rule out.

decision_rules.description: Signs suggestive of large vessel occlusion stroke
decision_rules.evidence_text: LVO strokes account for 24-46% of ischemic strokes but cause most disability. NIHSS >= 6 suggests LVO. Thrombectomy beneficial up to 24 hours.

action.intervention: BP management, reverse anticoagulation if applicable
action.rationale: Hemorrhage requires different management than ischemic stroke

decision_rules.evidence_text: ICH accounts for 10-15% of strokes but 30-50% of stroke mortality. Cannot distinguish from ischemic clinically - CT required.

tests: MRI preferred over CT for posterior fossa
action.rationale: Posterior strokes often missed, high mortality if basilar occlusion

decision_rules.evidence_text: Posterior circulation strokes are commonly missed. The 5 Ds: Dizziness, Diplopia, Dysarthria, Dysphagia, Dystaxia suggest posterior involvement.

clarifying_questions.question: When did the symptoms start? What time was the patient last seen normal?
clarifying_questions.question_zh: 症状什么时候开始的？患者最后一次正常是什么时候？

clarifying_questions.question: Is one side of the face drooping? Can the patient smile evenly?
clarifying_questions.question_zh: 脸的一侧是否下垂？患者能否均匀地微笑？

clarifying_questions.question: Is there weakness in one arm or leg? Can the patient raise both arms?
clarifying_questions.question_zh: 一侧手臂或腿有无力感吗？患者能否举起双臂？

clarifying_questions.question: Is speech slurred or difficult to understand?
clarifying_questions.question_zh: 说话是否含糊或难以理解？

clarifying_questions.question: Is this the worst headache of the patient's life? Did it start suddenly?
clarifying_questions.question_zh: 这是患者一生中最严重的头痛吗？是突然开始的吗？

text_chunks.title: FAST Stroke Recognition
text_chunks.content: FAST is a mnemonic for rapid stroke recognition: F - Face drooping (ask to smile, look for asymmetry), A - Arm weakness (ask to raise both arms, look for drift), S - Speech difficulty (ask to repeat a phrase, listen for slurring), T - Time to call emergency services (note time symptoms started). If ANY of F, A, or S is positive, stroke probability is high and immediate evaluation is needed. Time is Brain - 1.9 million neurons die per minute in untreated stroke.

text_chunks.title: Stroke Treatment Time Windows
text_chunks.content: Stroke treatment is time-sensitive: IV alteplase (tPA) can be given up to 4.5 hours from last known well time (reduces disability NNT=10). Mechanical thrombectomy for large vessel occlusion effective up to 24 hours in selected patients based on imaging. Door-to-needle time goal: < 60 minutes. Door-to-groin time goal: < 90 minutes. Earlier treatment = better outcomes. 'Time is Brain' - every 15-minute delay reduces benefit.

text_chunks.title: Stroke Red Flags
text_chunks.content: Stroke red flags requiring immediate action: (1) Any sudden neurological deficit, (2) Sudden severe headache (thunderclap), (3) Sudden vision loss, (4) Sudden confusion or difficulty speaking, (5) Sudden difficulty walking or loss of balance, (6) Sudden numbness, especially on one side. Additional concerning features: decreasing level of consciousness, seizure, high blood pressure (>220/120), symptoms fluctuating or worsening.

text_chunks.title: Stroke Mimics
text_chunks.content: Stroke mimics account for 15-30% of suspected strokes: (1) Hypoglycemia - check glucose immediately, (2) Seizure with post-ictal paralysis (Todd's paralysis), (3) Complex migraine with aura, (4) Conversion disorder, (5) Hypertensive encephalopathy, (6) Brain tumor, (7) Encephalitis, (8) Drug toxicity. Key differentiators: gradual onset, history of similar episodes, positive symptoms (tingling vs numbness), full deficit at onset (stroke) vs progressive (mimic).

text_chunks.title: Acute Stroke Management
text_chunks.content: Acute stroke management: (1) ABCs - maintain airway, breathing, circulation, (2) Check glucose - treat if < 60 mg/dL, (3) Obtain non-contrast CT Head STAT, (4) If ischemic and within 4.5 hours: IV alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (max 90mg), 10% bolus then 90% over 60 min, (5) If LVO suspected: CTA for thrombectomy evaluation, (6) For hemorrhage: reverse anticoagulation, BP control (target <140 systolic), consider surgery if cerebellar or large, (7) NPO until swallow evaluation, (8) Admit to stroke unit.
